verdicts.why: readTable (line 139) -> readFieldValue case 'F'/'A' (lines 181, 184) -> readArray (line 237) -> readFieldValue (line 245) is genuine mutual recursion with no depth counter anywhere in the file; a nesting level costs only 5 wire bytes ('A' + 4-byte length), so a few tens of KB - well inside one 128KB AMQP frame - yields thousands of stack frames, and nothing in the file catches the resulting StackOverflowError.

Lines 86-89 are quoted correctly and the only guard, `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE`, still admits 2147483646, so `new byte[(int)contentLength]` at line 88 allocates and zeroes the full declared size BEFORE `in.readFully(buffer)` at line 89 verifies any of those bytes exist on the wire; I found no other bound in the file and no caller-side clamp inside the target.

The anchor is right: line 86 reads a wire-supplied unsigned 32-bit length and line 88 allocates it with only a 2GB ceiling, before readFully validates it, reachable from readFieldValue cases 'S' (line 163) and 'x' (line 211); the cited lines 142/240 are the table/array length reads rather than the readBytes call sites and 'large table length' does not itself allocate, but those are citation imprecisions, not errors about the allocation defect.

No allocation is proportional to tableLength: lines 145-147 create an empty HashMap and two fixed-size stream wrappers, and TruncatedInputStream holds tableLength only as a remaining-bytes counter (the claim itself concedes it 'will eventually stop'), while the loop at line 148 is bounded by bytes actually available, so a huge declared length costs nothing - the HashMap only grows with bytes the attacker really sends.

The 'read past the intended boundary' half is refuted outright - the TruncatedInputStream wrappers at lines 146-147 and 241-242 enforce the limit regardless of available() - but whether available() can under-report and exit the loops at lines 148/244 early depends entirely on TruncatedInputStream's available() override and on which stream the (public) constructor at line 57 is handed, and neither source is under the target path.

Lines 240-243 allocate nothing proportional to `length` - it is passed to TruncatedInputStream as a byte counter, and the ArrayList starts empty and grows only per element actually parsed at lines 244-246, so 'reading 4GB' requires the attacker to actually transmit 4GB (bandwidth-bound), unlike readBytes line 88 which allocates the declared size before any data arrives.
